prompt: Why did `hq.key` come out as `-rw-------`?
hint: Look at what ran in front of `wg genkey`.

choices.text: wg genkey writes every key file that way
choices.why: It writes to standard output; the file's mode came from the shell that created it.

choices.text: sudo makes the files it creates private
choices.why: `hq.pub` was also written through sudo, with `tee`, and it is `-rw-r--r--`.

choices.text: The umask 077 set just before it
choices.why: Right. It removes every permission for group and others from files created in that shell.

choices.text: /etc/wireguard imposes that mode on its contents
choices.why: A directory does not set its files' mode; `hq.pub` sits beside it readable by all.

prompt: What in `hq`'s `wg0.conf` identifies the branch office?
hint: What would a stranger have to steal to pass as `branch`?

choices.text: The comment `# the branch office`
choices.why: A comment is for people; `wg` never reads or prints it.

choices.text: The public key in its peer block
choices.why: Right. Whoever holds the matching private key is `branch`, as far as `hq` is concerned.
The endpoint says where to send. A packet from that address under the wrong key is not accepted.

choices.text: A user name and password sent in the handshake
choices.why: WireGuard has no users and no passwords, only keys.

prompt: The peer `# Ana, at home` has no `Endpoint` line in `hq`'s file. What follows from that?
hint: Where could `hq` possibly learn her address?

choices.text: wg-quick refuses to bring wg0 up until one is added
choices.why: wg0 came up with that peer exactly as it was.

choices.text: hq sends her packets to 10.20.0.3 across the internet
choices.why: 10.20.0.3 is her tunnel address, which no internet router can reach.

choices.text: hq reaches her only after she has sent it a packet
choices.why: Right. The endpoint is learnt from her first authenticated packet.

choices.text: Her traffic has to go through branch, which has one
choices.why: Peers talk to each other directly; nothing relays her through the branch.

prompt: The banner said wireguard-go is not required because this kernel has first-class support for WireGuard. What is true of the kernel the lesson's transcript was recorded on?
hint: Read the line just above the banner.

choices.text: It has the module, and wireguard-go ran anyway
choices.why: `ip link add wg0 type wireguard` failed with `Unknown device type`.

choices.text: It lacks the module, so the banner is wrong here
choices.why: Right. The kernel had refused the device one line earlier; the banner is written for the ordinary kernel since 5.6.

choices.text: It predates 5.6, when WireGuard joined Linux
choices.why: It was a kernel compiled without the module, not an old one.

choices.text: It runs WireGuard in the kernel and in wireguard-go at once
choices.why: One implementation serves wg0, and here it is wireguard-go.

prompt: In the capture, how many packets did the WireGuard handshake between `hq` and `branch` take before data flowed?
hint: Count the ones that are not Transport Data.

prompt: The first reply through the new tunnel took 2.85 ms and the second 0.944 ms. Why the difference?
hint: WireGuard sends nothing until there is something to send.

choices.text: The first request was lost and sent again
choices.why: Nothing was lost: `icmp_seq=1` was answered.

choices.text: The ISP's link is slower for a first packet
choices.why: No link in the lab has any delay at all.

choices.text: The till answers its first ping more slowly
choices.why: Nothing on the till differs between the two; what differs is the tunnel.

choices.text: It waited for the handshake
choices.why: Right. WireGuard held the packet until the session keys existed, and did not drop it.

prompt: `wg show` on `hq` reported 404 B sent to the branch. Which packets make up that number?
hint: `wg` counts UDP payload, not what the wire carries.

choices.text: The initiation and the response on the wire, 190 + 134, plus padding
choices.why: The response was received, not sent, and those sizes include Ethernet, IP and UDP.

choices.text: 148 + 128 + 128: the initiation and two data packets
choices.why: Right. 190 − 42 and 170 − 42, with Ethernet, IP and UDP headers taken off.

choices.text: Two data packets of 170 and a 64-byte keepalive
choices.why: hq sends no keepalive, and 170 is the size with every outer header counted.

choices.text: Four equal packets of 101 bytes
choices.why: No packet in the capture was 101 bytes, and they were not all the same size.

prompt: Every WireGuard data packet carries a ___ that goes up by one per packet, so a recorded packet cannot be played back later.
hint: `tshark` printed it as 0 on the first one.

prompt: On `branch`, `hq`'s AllowedIPs was cut to `10.20.0.1/32` and the laptop's ping failed. Where was it dropped?
hint: The route and the keys were untouched.

choices.text: At hq, which had lost its route into wg0
choices.why: `192.168.20.0/24 dev wg0` was still on hq.

choices.text: At branch, once it was decrypted
choices.why: Right. Its source, 192.168.10.20, was no longer in the list for hq's key.

choices.text: At the ISP, which filters UDP 51820
choices.why: The same port carried the handshake and everything else all lesson.

choices.text: At the till, which rejected the laptop's address
choices.why: The till never received the packet.

prompt: `hq`'s firewall lets `192.168.20.0/24` reach `files`. Why is that a rule about the branch, and not about anybody who writes that source address into a packet?
hint: What had to happen to a packet before it came out of wg0?

choices.text: Private ranges cannot be forged on the internet
choices.why: A private source is as easy to write as any other.

choices.text: The ISP filters packets with spoofed sources
choices.why: The ISP never sees the inner addresses at all.

choices.text: From that range, only branch's key is accepted
choices.why: Right. A packet out of wg0 with that source was decrypted with branch's key and checked against its row.

choices.text: The tunnel hides the source address from hq
choices.why: hq reads the source after decryption; the rule depends on it.

prompt: What does a peer's AllowedIPs decide on `hq`? Choose all that apply.
hint: It is read going out and coming in, and wg-quick reads it too.

choices.text: Which peer an outgoing packet is encrypted for
choices.why: Right: the destination picks the row, and the row picks the key.

choices.text: Which source addresses are accepted from that peer
choices.why: Right: branch dropped the laptop's ping on exactly this.

choices.text: Which addresses the peer is permitted to reach
choices.why: That is the reading the name invites, and not what it does.

choices.text: Which routes wg-quick adds for wg0
choices.why: Right: `192.168.20.0/24 dev wg0` came from it.

choices.text: The UDP port the peer listens on
choices.why: That is ListenPort, or the port in Endpoint.

prompt: `hq`'s file has no Endpoint for Ana, yet `wg show` lists `198.51.100.77:40817`. Where did that come from?
hint: Nobody typed it.

choices.text: From resolving vpn.example.com
choices.why: That name is how she finds hq, not how hq finds her.

choices.text: From homegw's NAT table, read over the tunnel by hq
choices.why: hq has no way to read another router's tables.

choices.text: From her first packet that authenticated
choices.why: Right. The address and port it came from became her endpoint, the home router's NAT included.

choices.text: From her AllowedIPs, 10.20.0.3/32
choices.why: That is her tunnel address, and hq's own file already has it.

prompt: Which machine needed `PersistentKeepalive = 25`, and why?
hint: Which of them sits behind a router that forgets?

choices.text: hq, so branch knows the office is alive
choices.why: WireGuard sends no liveness messages between fixed addresses, and needs none.

choices.text: The laptop, so homegw keeps its NAT mapping
choices.why: Right. Idle, the home router forgets the port, and hq could no longer reach her.

choices.text: Both ends, or the handshake expires
choices.why: A handshake is renewed by traffic, not by keepalives.

choices.text: branch, because its Endpoint line is fixed
choices.why: A fixed public address is the case that needs no keepalive.

prompt: With the wrong key, the ISP saw initiations at 0 and at 5.277388 seconds. Roughly every how many seconds is an unanswered initiation sent again?
hint: Round to the nearest whole second.

prompt: With the wrong key on Ana's side, why did `hq` send nothing back, not even an error?
hint: What would `hq` need in order to answer?

choices.text: It cannot authenticate the initiation, and stays silent
choices.why: Right. A WireGuard endpoint does not answer a packet it cannot authenticate, which also hides it from scanners.

choices.text: The ISP blocks traffic towards port 51820
choices.why: The two initiations crossed the ISP; its own capture shows them.

choices.text: hq's wg0 was down during the test
choices.why: It had been restarted and was up; the right key would have been answered.

choices.text: WireGuard reports errors over TCP, which was blocked
choices.why: WireGuard uses UDP alone and has no error message to send.

prompt: Ana's laptop moves from home to a hotel with the tunnel up. Put what happens in order.
hint: hq believes a new address only after one thing.
items: The laptop sends its next packet from the hotel's address
hq authenticates it under Ana's key
hq moves her endpoint to the new address
hq's replies go to the hotel
trap: The endpoint moves only after the packet authenticates; an address alone proves nothing.

prompt: With `tls-crypt` on, what could `tshark` at the ISP still recognise?
hint: Read the first two lines of the capture.

choices.text: The Client Hello and the server's certificate
choices.why: Those are what disappeared: after two packets it saw only Continuation Data.

choices.text: Nothing at all: it saw plain UDP
choices.why: It named the first two packets OpenVPN, by their message type.

choices.text: The user name ana, from her certificate
choices.why: The name appeared only in the server's own status file and log.

choices.text: That it was OpenVPN, from the two HARD_RESET packets
choices.why: Right. The message type stays readable; the TLS inside does not.

prompt: Somebody leaves the company. On this OpenVPN server, what cuts off her access and nobody else's?
hint: Which of these belongs to her alone?

choices.text: A new tc.key on the server
choices.why: Every client shares that key: a new one locks everybody out until it is handed round again.

choices.text: Removing her line from server.conf and restarting it
choices.why: server.conf has no line per user; any certificate the authority signed connects.

choices.text: Revoking her certificate, checked with crl-verify
choices.why: Right. Her certificate is her identity, and nobody else's changes.

choices.text: Moving the pool off 10.8.0.0/24
choices.why: The pool hands addresses to whoever authenticates; it decides nothing about who.

prompt: Match each value from the OpenVPN capture to what it is.
hint: Status file, pool and key.

pairs.right: The Common Name in her certificate
homegw's address and a port its NAT chose
Her address from the server's pool
A key every client holds a copy of

right_distractors: A key that only Ana holds

prompt: In the status file, `ana` is the Common ___ of the certificate she connected with.
hint: The first column's heading.

prompt: A new branch joins over WireGuard. `wg show` on `hq` shows its handshake 20 seconds ago, but the branch's PCs cannot reach `files`. What is the likeliest fix?
hint: A recent handshake rules out one whole family of causes.

choices.text: New key pairs on both routers
choices.why: A handshake only completes when the keys are right.

choices.text: PersistentKeepalive on hq
choices.why: Keepalives hold NAT mappings open; this handshake already works.

choices.text: The branch LAN added to that peer's AllowedIPs on hq
choices.why: Right. Without it, hq drops the PCs' packets on arrival, as branch did in this lesson.

choices.text: A lower MTU on wg0
choices.why: An MTU fault lets small packets through; here nothing gets through.

prompt: The network team links two routers it manages itself. Which fits better, and why?
hint: Who is at each end?

choices.text: OpenVPN, because WireGuard cannot carry a whole LAN
choices.why: It carried 192.168.20.0/24 through this whole lesson.

choices.text: WireGuard, since one key per router is all the identity needed
choices.why: Right. There are no people to name or revoke, and the file is short enough to check by eye.

choices.text: OpenVPN over TCP, as UDP is too unreliable for a tunnel
choices.why: UDP is the normal carrier for a tunnel; TCP inside TCP is the trouble lesson 3 describes.

choices.text: Neither: a link between routers needs IPsec
choices.why: IPsec is one option, lesson 2's, not a requirement.
